Overall, the reviewers found this work interesting. The reported results provide a potentially exciting link between two rapidly evolving domains in computational and cognitive neuroscience. The authors employ some clever analyses; the dissociation between state uncertainty and action variability, in particular, is a nice feature of the analysis.

But all reviewers also raised substantial concerns, of either conceptual or technical nature, which would need to be addressed before this paper can be reconsidered for publication at eLife. The conceptual concerns hover around the mechanistic interpretation of the results: reviewers did not feel like the modeling, and the link between model and physiology, were as clear as they could have been.

We realize that addressing all the essential points below might be challenging within the relatively short period of time intended for the revision process at eLife, and hence we would like you to prepare a response and action plan.

Essential revisions:

1) Please provide a detailed model-based analysis of participants' behavior, ideally comparing the current model to other plausible ones.

Currently, none of your analyses shows how well the model accounts for participants' behavior. The model doesn't even define a policy, so it doesn't address the explore-exploit trade-off directly. Modeling behavior is important both in order to state clearly a mechanistic hypothesis about choice behavior, and to show empirically that such a model is supported by the data.

Modeling behavior would be critical, for example, to determine whether the representational change in OFC reflects some multi-faceted entropy measure as might be predicted by a "state" account of OFC representation, or over-representation of an error signal during periods of high arousal, which would also be consistent with ideas about value signals in OFC.

By the same token, your primary behavioral figure shows that participants switched more under conditions of high entropy, but this is quite highly correlated with the actual trial outcome. Does the model-based entropy measure affect participant behavior beyond simple win-stay lose-shift or reinforcement learning effects? If so, what are the additional aspects of task environment (e.g. feedback validity, prior feedback history) that jointly affect entropy measures and switching behavior?

2) Please unpack your mechanistic reasoning with regards to entropy. You put forward the idea (i) that posterior uncertainty always decreases with more observations, and therefore (ii) that some specific mechanism must "drive up entropy" in dynamic environments, and they look for such a mechanism in this paper. The reviewers understand this can be an interpretation of a leaky accumulation process, in which the leak "drives up entropy" (ii) and the accumulation "decreases posterior uncertainty" (i). But it is not entirely clear from the perspective of Bayesian inference. Specifically, reviewers raised two issues in this context.

2a) It is not generally true that posterior entropy decreases with more observations.

You state (Introduction): "if beliefs about the environment are expressed as a posterior distribution over possible states, the entropy, or uncertainty, of this posterior decreases as the number of concordant data points increases." Whether or not this is a mathematically correct statement depends on what is meant by "concordant" (which does not seem to be a technical concept). There are plenty of cases where posterior entropy will increase as more data arrive. For example, if you initially strongly believe that a coin is biased to produce heads and then you observe tails, then your posterior will be higher entropy than your prior. (This also comes up later on the same page: "If the 'leak' were removed, the model entropy would still decrease with each new observation, as this is a natural consequence of gaining information").

2b) It is not clear why a dedicated mechanism would be required to "drive up" or "inject" entropy.

Reviewers do not understand why a Bayesian model of inference must "counter" inflexibility by "injecting" entropy. There is nothing, mathematically speaking, that requires a model of (presumably human) inference to inject entropy. Also, talking about mechanisms like "leak" seem to be confusing algorithmic/implementational level concerns with the computational-level analysis of the internal probabilistic model (see point 3a below). The "leak" in the Behrens et al. (2007) model, for example, comes directly from assumptions about volatility; it's not a mechanism that is "injected" into the model to increase entropy. The two computations called (i) and (ii) above are a direct consequence of probability calculus (subsection “Bayesian learning model”). Equation 6 in subsection “Bayesian learning model” shows that the assumption of non-stationarity (s > 0) counterbalances, and may even override, the decrease in posterior uncertainty by constantly injecting a uniform prior in the inference. There is no need to further "drive up entropy". Thus, reviewers feel that the statement in the Introduction: "… injecting uncertainty back into the model's state estimate to make rapid changes of belief possible" needs to be qualified or dropped.

3) There are other mechanistic concepts and related terminology, which should be clarified.

3a) In general, the Introduction tends to conflate the computational level of analysis with the level of the biological mechanisms. Reviewers feel it would help to more carefully separate those two.

3b) In choosing your definition of exploitation, you try to rely on "as few assumptions or arbitrary cut-offs as possible" (Results section). Reviewers don't think that's possible. The definition of exploitation you adopted (the first trial on which participants selected the true high reward probability option and received reward) is arguably just as arbitrary as other sensible definitions. An agent in an exploratory mode will place some probability on this option, and hence its selection does not reliably indicate exploitation. Assumptions are inescapable, and it's better to adopt a model-based definition. But until the policy is defined explicitly, this is not possible.

3c) Reviewers do not understand the statement that uncertainty increases on unrewarded trials (subsection “Noradrenaline as a candidate mechanism for increasing flexibility of belief representations”). It's mathematically possible (though relatively unlikely) that uncertainty will increase on unrewarded trials, if subjects have low confidence during an exploitation phase.

3d) The following statement (Introduction) may be incorrect depending on how one interprets the terminology: "the better established one's model of the environment, the less flexible one's beliefs are." This depends on what "flexible" and "established" mean. If flexibility means something like the degree to which the posterior can deviate from the prior when new data arrive (e.g., expected KL-divergence), and if "established" means lower prior entropy, then one can conceive situations where the claim is incorrect.

4) Please elaborate on the decoding analysis.

4a) You look for a region that shows "stronger [decoded] representation strength for the currently selected option when model entropy is low", which should be a hallmark of a probabilistic model. It would be more natural to look for the posterior distribution of option values, rather than a representation of the selection option. It actually looks like it is the representation decoded in mOFC here. Indeed, if the representation decoded is that of the selected option, then it does not really make sense that the classifier's probability is actually lowest for the current option (compared to other options) in the high entropy condition (Figure 2C). By contrast, this result is expected for the option value. As seen on Figure 1C, when posterior entropy is highest in exploitation periods (the ones analyzed here), the value of the currently selected option tends to be the lowest.

4b) From the same basic perspective, the representational analyses could better clarify the source of the effects, rather than lumping everything into entropy. A difference in decoding reliability driven by differences in error versus correct trials is a rather different effect than one that emerges across feedback-validity conditions when accounting statistically for feedback history. The error versus correct distinction is one where the difference in frequency of these two conditions might lead to artificially low estimates of decoding reliability in error trials, which, given larger pupil responses on error trials, could make interpretation of the OFC pupil results fairly tricky. By this token, one could argue that a number of the findings reported in OFC [general uncertainty, choice-specific belief, and 70% vs 90% in the same regions (subsection “Medial OFC represents probabilistic beliefs about the state of the environment” and Figure 2—supplement 1)] could all be driven by a conjunctive code over feedback and option value, rather than by the tracking of reliability weighted state representations.

5) Please substantiate claims about temporal precedence.

The results are interpreted in terms of temporal precedence with the implicit assumption being that pupil diameter prior to outcome presentation relates to subsequent reliability of OFC representations. However, since pupil diameter, BOLD responses, and entropy all likely contain fairly strong autocorrelations, it would be useful if you could better test this assumption by determining whether the relationships hold even after shifting the pupil and OFC signals in time relative to one another (e.g. does OFC representation reliability predict pupil diameter on subsequent trial?).

6) Please provide a more comprehensive characterization of LC responses, and the methods used to detect them.

You should show the actual response time courses, rather than only statistical maps. You should also show the correlation between the LC and pupil responses. There is a dispute in the literature about the feasibility of LC imaging and the pitfalls and physiological artefacts (e.g. Astafiev, 2010; de Gee et al., 2017). Please also provide more information in Materials and methods section – did you correct for physiological noise (using RETROICOR or related approaches)? If not, it might be better to take the LC findings out altogether and focus on the pupil. Finally, some of your claims seem to require that the effects should specific to the LC-NA system. Substantiating this claim would require contrasting LC responses to responses of other brainstem regions.

7) Please elaborate on the representation of the relevant prior literature.

There is a whole literature on this topic, which is only scarcely referred to. The following references (potentially more) should be included:

– Iigaya, 2016 presents a mechanistic view for driving up entropy with noradrenaline, with the idea that a surprise detection module is used to reset (by means of noradrenaline) the representation currently hold and stored in synapses.

– Meyniel and Dehaene, 2017 for waning and waxing of posterior uncertainty and its neural (fMRI) representation

– Pulcu and Browning, 2017 on pupil size variations with volatility

– Krishnamurthy, Nassar and Gold, 2017 on a link between pupil size and the balance between prior and current evidence in uncertain environments

– de Gee et al., 2017 for showing that fMRI responses in the human LC, but also other neuromodulatory brainstem nuclei, correlate with pupil dilation. In that regard, please tone down the statement that pupil dilation is a specific marker of LC activity (how specific this link is, has rarely been tested directly and the few studies that did, in humans, monkey, and rodents, founds links to several brainstem systems).

[Editors' note: further revisions were requested prior to acceptance, as described below.]

Thank you for resubmitting your article "Control of entropy in neural models of environmental state" for further consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by a Reviewing Editor, a Senior Editor and three peer reviewers.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below.

Summary:

All three reviewers and the Reviewing Editor were overall happy with the revisions and think that the paper has become much clearer. All remain convinced that the paper addresses an important and interesting topic. One reviewer still voiced three major concerns and suggested ways of addressing them through textual revisions, plus one possible additional analysis. We feel that addressing these points through textual revisions, and toning down certain parts of the conclusions, would be essential for publication. We leave it to the authors to decide whether or not perform the additional analysis suggested.

Essential revisions:

1) Mathematical constructs that motivate the study and analysis.

The authors now clearly decompose the inference into (1) computing a posterior distribution and (2) turning this posterior distribution into a predictive distribution by applying a transition-function which, if volatility is assumed, blunts the posterior. Using this (clear) terminology, they then say, "we investigate the hypothesis that the brain has a mechanism for increasing entropy in internal models that is analogous to the transition-function update described above". It seems that their analysis cannot be in line with this, since in their experiment, volatility (the rate of change) is constant, therefore the transition-function is constant, and it is impossible to correlate a brain/pupil signal with it or claim that a brain mechanism has been found for it. We suggest further editing the Introduction clarify this aspect.

2) Effect of entropy on representation strength.

It remains that the decoding results are not fully in line with the cartoon illustration in Figure 1B, in particular, that decoding is not significant in the high entropy condition. Instead, it looks like an effect of value, and indeed the effect is significant in GLM 4 testing reward probability.

We are concerned that the control (point 4, second part, in the response letter) for the contribution of value may not have been adequate. They regressed out, voxel-wise, the linear effect of value. The analysis in the (univariate) residuals does not preclude that there remains multivariate activity related to value, which, if correlated with entropy, will boost the effect of entropy. The conserve approach may be more appropriate: value should be regressed out from entropy, then if the correlation between representation strength (derived from the decoder) and residual entropy remains significant and negative, it will be convincing that the effect is not confounded by value.

We realize that this control analysis may not be possible with the current design (strong negative correlation between value and entropy) – if that is the case, then the claim about a specific involvement of entropy should be toned down.

3) Effect of noradrenaline.

The authors opted for removing the LC-fMRI results about which we had technical concerns. So, their claim about noradrenaline now relies entirely on the pupil data, but this overly specific conclusion is not supported by the available data. Specifically, the authors quote Joshi et al., 2016 to relate baseline pupil size (which is central in their analysis) to noradrenaline levels, but the quoted paper in fact shows that LC activity is specifically related to changes in pupil size. Reimer et al., 2016 go further in showing that pupil dynamics is correlated to both, noradrenaline and acetylcholine-release, and the former is more strongly related to the fast dilations of the pupil whereas the latter is more strongly related to slow variations in pupil size, which would correspond to fluctuations in baseline pupil size in the current paper. The authors should refrain from linking their results specifically to the LC-NA system; they should link their results to "pupil-linked arousal". They can go on to speculate that the LC-NA system might play a key role in their findings, but then they would need to acknowledge that their slow baseline pupil size effects would be more in line with a cholinergic effect. It does not seem to match well with the influential accounts in this field, but we need to take this recent evidence from careful experiments into neuromodulatory correlates of pupil dynamics seriously.

results.result: Participants performed a 4-arm bandit task where they alternated between exploitation (72% of trials, mean block length 13.7 trials) and exploration phases. Model entropy was high during exploitation and low during exploration, and both high entropy and high relative uncertainty predicted switching from exploitation to exploration following reward omission. The computational model predicted 95% of exploit trials and 51% of explore trials correctly.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C30 provide converging behavioral and model-based evidence. The task design is clearly described (C20-C21), behavioral patterns are quantified with appropriate statistics (C22-C25), model entropy relationships are demonstrated (C26-C27), and statistical tests show significant effects (C28-C29 with p<0.001). Model validation shows good predictive accuracy (C30), supporting the validity of the computational approach.

results.result: Exploration and exploitation phases engaged distinct brain networks: exploration activated frontal-parietal networks and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, while exploitation engaged medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC) and hippocampus. Response switching and high model entropy predicted activity in frontal-parietal and dorsomedial frontal cortex, while low model entropy predicted mOFC and hippocampus activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C37 describe univariate fMRI results from GLM1 and GLM2 analyses. The findings are supported by appropriate statistical analyses and are consistent with prior literature on model-based choice (C33). The dissociation between exploration and exploitation networks is clearly demonstrated, though the results are primarily descriptive rather than mechanistic.

results.result: Multivariate fMRI analysis identified a region in mOFC where representation strength for the chosen option was higher when model entropy was lower (p<0.05 corrected). This effect survived multiple comparisons correction, remained significant after controlling for value and reward history, and was distinct from action/policy representations in motor and visual cortex. A similar but weaker effect was observed in hippocampus (uncorrected p<0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C48 describe the core multivariate fMRI finding. The result is well-supported with appropriate multiple comparisons correction (C40-C41), control analyses ruling out confounds from value and reward history (C47-C48), and validation using alternative measures (C46). The authors appropriately note the hippocampus effect did not survive correction (C43). The interpretation as a probabilistic state representation (C44-C45) is reasonable given the data.

results.result: Pupil diameter was larger during exploration than exploitation and increased following reward omission. Critically, increases in baseline pupil size predicted decreases in mOFC representation strength specifically on unrewarded trials (t(15)=-2.94, p=0.01) but not rewarded trials (t(15)=0.37, p=0.71), with a significant difference between conditions (t(15)=2.82, p=0.01). This relationship was temporally specific and remained significant after controlling for value.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C62 provide strong evidence for the pupil-mOFC relationship. The directional specificity (increases but not decreases in entropy, C54-C58) is well-demonstrated with appropriate statistics. Control analyses confirm temporal specificity (C59) and robustness to confounds (C60). The effect replicates in explore trials (C61) and is illustrated with median split analysis (C62). The finding that uncertainty increases occurred almost exclusively after reward omissions (C57: 0.2% after rewards) strengthens the interpretation.

results.result: ACC activity was directionally sensitive to changes in entropy, being more active when entropy increased. ACC activity predicted changes in baseline pupil diameter (p<0.05 corrected), over and above effects of entropy changes and mean brain activity. However, there was no direct relationship between ACC activity and changes in mOFC representation strength (p>0.1).
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64, C67-C68, and C88 describe the ACC findings with appropriate statistical corrections. The lack of direct ACC-mOFC relationship (C68) is honestly reported and may reflect measurement noise. The interpretation connecting to prior literature (C65, C81-C82) is reasonable. The results support a model where ACC influences mOFC indirectly via neuromodulatory systems, though the evidence is correlational rather than causal.

results.result: The study provides evidence for top-down neuromodulatory control of entropy in neural state models, where pupil diameter (indexing neuromodulatory state) predicted increases in entropy in mOFC, and ACC activity predicted pupil diameter. This suggests neuromodulatory systems play a crucial role in implementing flexibility of internal representations during decision-making.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8 and C79-C80, C84, C96 represent the main conclusions synthesizing the empirical findings. The evidence chain (ACC → pupil → mOFC entropy) is well-supported by the individual results, though the interpretation regarding neuromodulation must be qualified given that pupil diameter reflects multiple neuromodulators and arousal factors (acknowledged in C77). The conclusions are appropriately cautious about causal mechanisms.

results.result: While pupil diameter is used to index neuromodulatory state including noradrenaline, it depends on multiple neuromodulators (noradrenaline and acetylcholine) and other arousal factors. Prior work has proposed noradrenaline as a mechanism for controlling uncertainty in neural models, with experimental evidence showing it increases behavioral randomness and reduces selectivity of cortical representations.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C17-C19, C77-C78 appropriately contextualize the pupillometry measure and its limitations. The authors correctly note that pupil diameter cannot be linked directly to noradrenaline (C77) and cite relevant prior work. This represents appropriate scientific caution about the interpretation of the pupillometry results, though it somewhat limits the specificity of the mechanistic claims.

results.result: The study is grounded in established theoretical frameworks showing that internal models represent uncertainty about environmental states, which controls learning rates and choice behavior. Theoretical models include mechanisms to increase model uncertainty (transition functions), and prior work has linked ACC activity to volatility, belief updating, and uncertainty.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C9-C16 provide theoretical background and literature review. These are well-supported by appropriate citations to established work in reinforcement learning, Bayesian inference, and prior neuroimaging studies. The theoretical framework is clearly articulated and provides appropriate context for the current study.

results.result: The mOFC representation is interpreted as consistent with prior proposals that this region represents current location in task state space and hidden task-relevant information. The authors speculate that different task domains might rely on probabilistic models in other cortical regions, and that the mOFC representation might reflect online rather than offline storage of contingencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C76 provide interpretation and speculation about the nature of mOFC representations. The connection to prior work (C72-C73) is appropriate, and the speculations (C74-C76) are clearly identified as such and are reasonable given the data. These claims appropriately acknowledge limitations in understanding the exact nature of the representation.

results.result: The authors consider and address an alternative explanation that ACC and pupil effects reflect drive for exploratory behavior rather than belief changes. They argue this cannot account for the pupil-mOFC relationship in the absence of behavioral change, and cite animal work showing noradrenaline reduces cortical selectivity. They propose a hypothesis distinguishing noradrenaline effects on ACC (behavioral stochasticity) versus mOFC (entropic beliefs).
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C94 demonstrate appropriate consideration of alternative explanations. The counterargument (C92) is logical given that the key pupil-mOFC effects were observed during stable exploitation behavior. The synthesis (C94) is presented as a hypothesis rather than established fact, which is appropriate. This represents good scientific reasoning about competing interpretations.

results.result: The study included 22 participants (19 in final fMRI analysis, 16 in pupil analysis after exclusions) who completed 1600 trials across two sessions. The computational model used Bayesian inference with a fixed switch probability of 1/20. fMRI data were acquired at 3T with multiband EPI. Multivariate analysis used PCA dimensionality reduction to 20 components, validated by permutation testing showing no bias.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C113 describe methods and validation analyses. Sample sizes are appropriate based on reported power analyses. The computational model is clearly specified (C103-C104). fMRI acquisition parameters are standard (C105-C106). The dimensionality reduction approach is justified (C107-C109) and validated with permutation testing (C110-C112) showing the method does not introduce spurious results. Methods are generally well-described and appropriate.

results.result: In the current task, state and option value are inherently interlinked because possible states correspond to which option is the high reward option. High confidence in the chosen option (low entropy) necessarily correlates strongly with that option having high expected value (r=-0.93±0.005).
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 acknowledge an important limitation of the task design where state identity and value are confounded. The authors appropriately note this correlation (C50) and discuss its implications. This represents appropriate transparency about the interpretation of their results, though it does limit the ability to dissociate state representation from value representation.

results.result: The authors acknowledge the study was not designed to dissociate ACC's role in belief updating from other proposed functions (cognitive control, choice difficulty). They note that while ACC-noradrenaline coordination has been theoretically proposed and anatomically plausible, direct evidence during belief updating tasks has been lacking. The results suggest different mechanisms for forming versus revising beliefs.
results.evaluation: Claims C83, C85-C87, C95 appropriately acknowledge limitations and contextualize the findings. The authors correctly note they cannot dissociate between alternative ACC theories (C83) and that their evidence is correlational rather than causal. The acknowledgment of gaps in prior literature (C87) and speculation about mechanisms (C85, C95) are appropriately qualified.

results.result: The authors propose that theoretical models require a dedicated mechanism to drive up entropy to maintain flexibility, and that noradrenaline serves this role through a 'network reset' mechanism.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised substantial concerns about the mechanistic reasoning (Essential revision 2), questioning whether a dedicated mechanism is mathematically required to 'inject' entropy and noting confusion between computational and implementational levels. They state 'it is not clear why a dedicated mechanism would be required to drive up or inject entropy' and that assumptions about volatility naturally produce entropy changes without additional mechanisms.

results.result: Pupil diameter, indexing neuromodulatory state including noradrenaline, predicted increases (but not decreases) in entropy in mOFC representations, specifically on unrewarded trials where uncertainty increases.
results.evaluation: While reviewers found the dissociation between state uncertainty and action variability 'a nice feature,' they raised major concerns in the second round (Essential revision 3) that the link to noradrenaline specifically is not supported, noting that baseline pupil size relates more to acetylcholine than noradrenaline. They state authors 'should refrain from linking their results specifically to the LC-NA system' and instead link to 'pupil-linked arousal.'

results.result: A region in mOFC showed stronger representation of the chosen option when model entropy was lower, consistent with a probabilistic internal model where representation strength is modulated by uncertainty.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised concerns about whether this reflects entropy versus value effects (Essential revision 4b and second round Essential revision 2). They note 'it looks like an effect of value' and express concern that controls for value 'may not have been adequate,' suggesting the effect could be 'driven by a conjunctive code over feedback and option value' rather than entropy-weighted state representations. They recommend toning down claims if proper controls aren't possible.

results.result: ACC activity was directionally sensitive to changes in entropy and predicted subsequent changes in baseline pupil diameter, suggesting a role in signaling when beliefs should be updated.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings after revisions, with one noting the paper 'has become much clearer' in the second round. While they raised concerns about specificity to noradrenaline versus broader arousal systems, the core finding that ACC activity relates to entropy changes and pupil responses was not directly challenged.

results.result: Model entropy and relative uncertainty predicted participants' switching behavior, with the model correctly predicting 95% of exploit trials and 51% of explore trials.
results.evaluation: Reviewers requested detailed model-based analysis (Essential revision 1), questioning whether 'the model-based entropy measure affect participant behavior beyond simple win-stay lose-shift or reinforcement learning effects.' They noted the model 'doesn't even define a policy' and that modeling behavior is 'important both in order to state clearly a mechanistic hypothesis about choice behavior, and to show empirically that such a model is supported by the data.'

results.result: The relationship between pupil dilation and mOFC representation changes was temporally specific and robust to various control analyses including value regression and exploration trials.
results.evaluation: Reviewers requested temporal specificity tests (Essential revision 5), and the authors provided analyses showing effects disappeared when signals were shifted in time. These control analyses appear to have satisfied reviewer concerns about temporal precedence and autocorrelations.

results.result: Participants' behavior alternated between exploitation and exploration phases, with model entropy being generally high during exploitation and low during exploration, and higher when reward probability was lower.
results.evaluation: These basic behavioral characterizations were not challenged by reviewers. Their concerns focused on the mechanistic interpretation and modeling rather than the descriptive behavioral patterns.

results.result: Exploration engaged frontal-parietal and dorsomedial prefrontal networks, while exploitation engaged mOFC and hippocampus; entropy and switching predicted activity in these networks differentially.
results.evaluation: These univariate fMRI results identifying brain regions associated with exploration versus exploitation were not directly challenged by reviewers. Concerns focused on the multivariate decoding and mechanistic interpretations rather than these basic activation patterns.

results.result: Baseline pupil size was larger during exploration than exploitation, increased when transitioning to exploration, and showed sustained increases following reward omission.
results.evaluation: These basic pupillometry findings were not challenged by reviewers. Their concerns focused on the interpretation of what pupil changes represent (noradrenaline specifically versus broader arousal) rather than the measurements themselves.

results.result: The findings suggest pupil-linked neuromodulation reduces selectivity of cortical representations, potentially analogous to rodent work showing noradrenaline broadens tuning curves.
results.evaluation: In the second round (Essential revision 3), reviewers strongly criticized the specificity of linking to noradrenaline, noting that 'pupil dilation depends on at least two neuromodulators' and that baseline pupil effects 'would be more in line with a cholinergic effect.' They state the conclusion about noradrenaline specifically 'is not supported by the available data.'

results.result: The authors argue against an alternative explanation that ACC and pupil effects reflect only exploratory behavioral drive, proposing instead that noradrenaline has dual roles in behavioral stochasticity (via ACC) and belief entropy (via mOFC).
results.evaluation: While the authors present arguments against the alternative explanation, reviewers' concerns about the specificity of noradrenaline involvement (Essential revision 3, second round) and the potential confound with value signals (Essential revision 4b, second round revision 2) leave this mechanistic interpretation uncertain. The lack of direct ACC-mOFC relationship (C68) is noted but the overall mechanistic model remains incompletely validated.

results.result: Permutation analysis confirmed that the mOFC decoding results were not due to bias introduced by the PCA dimensionality reduction procedure.
results.evaluation: This methodological control was presented in response to potential concerns about the analysis pipeline. Reviewers did not challenge this specific control analysis, though they raised other concerns about what the decoding represents.

comparisons.comparison: Both address univariate fMRI findings (C31-C37). OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED with appropriate statistics, while peer reviewers also SUPPORTED these basic activation patterns without direct challenge. Agreement on descriptive findings, though reviewers focused concerns elsewhere on mechanistic interpretations.

Both address multivariate fMRI decoding of entropy (C40-C48). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED with appropriate controls for value and reward history. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAIN evaluation, raising concerns that effects may reflect value rather than entropy and that controls 'may not have been adequate.' Major disagreement on interpretation of what is being decoded.

Both address behavioral patterns (C22-C27). OpenEval finds behavioral evidence SUPPORTED with appropriate statistics. Peer reviewers also SUPPORTED these descriptive patterns without challenge. Strong agreement on basic behavioral characterizations.

OpenEval R1 includes model validation claims (C28-C30) that peer R5 addresses with UNCERTAIN evaluation. Reviewers questioned whether model-based entropy affects behavior beyond simple reinforcement learning and noted the model 'doesn't even define a policy.' OpenEval found evidence SUPPORTED; reviewers wanted more detailed model-based analysis.

Both address temporal specificity controls for pupil-mOFC relationship (C59-C62). OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED as appropriate controls. Peer reviewers also SUPPORTED after authors provided analyses showing effects disappeared with temporal shifts. Strong agreement on adequacy of temporal controls.

Both address basic pupillometry findings (C51-C53). OpenEval finds directional specificity SUPPORTED with strong statistics. Peer reviewers also SUPPORTED the measurements themselves without challenge. Agreement on the empirical pupil findings, though reviewers raised interpretation concerns addressed in other results.

OpenEval R4 addresses directional specificity of entropy increases (C54-C58) finding it SUPPORTED. Peer R2 addresses overlapping claims (C54-C56, C58) but expresses UNCERTAIN evaluation, questioning the link to noradrenaline specifically versus broader arousal. Disagreement on mechanistic interpretation despite agreement on the pattern.

Both address ACC findings (C63-C64, C67, C88). OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED with appropriate corrections. Peer reviewers also SUPPORTED the core ACC-entropy-pupil findings after revisions, noting the paper 'has become much clearer.' Agreement on ACC results despite concerns about noradrenaline specificity.

Both address mechanistic reasoning and pupillometry interpretation (C3-C4, C17, C19, C77). OpenEval finds the contextualization SUPPORTED as appropriate caution. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAIN evaluation, questioning whether a dedicated mechanism is mathematically required and noting confusion between computational and implementational levels. Disagreement on adequacy of mechanistic framework.

Both address limitations of pupil-noradrenaline link (C77-C78). OpenEval finds the caveats SUPPORTED as appropriate scientific caution. Peer R10 expresses UNCERTAIN evaluation, strongly criticizing the specificity to noradrenaline and noting baseline pupil effects 'would be more in line with a cholinergic effect.' Disagreement on whether caveats are sufficient.

OpenEval R6 addresses main conclusions (C6-C8, C79-C80, C84, C96) finding the evidence chain SUPPORTED. Peer R2 overlaps on C5-C6 and related mechanistic claims, expressing UNCERTAIN evaluation about the noradrenaline link. Major disagreement on whether conclusions are adequately supported.

Both address interpretation of neuromodulatory mechanisms (C79-C80). OpenEval finds conclusions SUPPORTED though appropriately cautious. Peer R10 expresses UNCERTAIN evaluation, stating the noradrenaline conclusion 'is not supported by the available data.' Disagreement on specificity of mechanistic claims.

Both address alternative explanations and mechanistic interpretation (C89-C94). OpenEval finds the consideration of alternatives SUPPORTED as good scientific reasoning. Peer R11 expresses UNCERTAIN evaluation, noting concerns about noradrenaline specificity and value confounds leave the mechanistic model incompletely validated. Disagreement on adequacy of mechanistic validation.

Both address methodological validation (C110-C112). OpenEval finds dimensionality reduction and permutation testing SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers also SUPPORTED this control analysis without challenge. Agreement on methodological adequacy of this specific control.

OpenEval R5 addresses lack of direct ACC-mOFC relationship (C68) as honestly reported. Peer R11 includes C68 in discussion of mechanistic uncertainty. Both note this limitation, though peer reviewers see it as part of broader concerns about the mechanistic model.

OpenEval R8 addresses theoretical background (C1-C3, C9-C16) finding it SUPPORTED. Peer R1 includes C3 in concerns about mechanistic reasoning, questioning the theoretical framework. Disagreement on adequacy of theoretical foundation.

OpenEval R9 addresses interpretation of mOFC representations (C72-C76) finding speculations appropriately qualified and SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific interpretive claims.

OpenEval R12 addresses task design limitation where state identity and value are confounded (C49-C50), finding the acknowledgment SUPPORTED as appropriate transparency. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though peer R3 raises related concerns about value confounds in different context.

OpenEval R13 addresses various limitations and contextualizations (C83, C85-C87, C95) finding them SUPPORTED as appropriately qualified. No direct corresponding peer review evaluation, though these limitations relate to concerns raised across multiple peer results.
